description: Prometheus and Loki responses reshaped into the field-based graph contract with ordinary dashboard transformations. Every fixture reproduces a real datasource frame shape: predictable_csv_wave is a metric query (one frame per series, value field named Value), csv_content is an instant query with Format: Table. One joinByField on Time does the widening; filter.byRefId separates two queries in one panel. The PromQL/LogQL is in every panel description.

options.content:
# Prometheus & Loki → relations charts

Every other relations dashboard in this repo hands the panel row-format CSV. This one
starts from **the frame shapes Prometheus and Loki actually return** and reaches the
field-based graph contract with ordinary dashboard transformations — the work a real
user has to do, which nothing else here shows.

**The rule:** *N series = N frames.* A `joinByField` on `Time` makes them **one wide
frame whose field names are the edge ids**, because `joinDataFrames` renames a field
called `Value` to its frame name and keeps its labels. Without the join the panel sees
only the **first** frame — one edge — because `findEdgesFrame` takes the first match.

| Fixture here | Is byte-for-byte | Which is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `predictable_csv_wave` | `meta.type: timeseries-multi`, one frame per series, frame name = legend format, value field named `Value` with the label set | a Prometheus/Loki **metric query**, `Format: Time series` |
| `csv_content` | one frame, `Time` as `time`, label columns as `string`, `Value` as `number` | a Prometheus **instant query**, `Format: Table` |

So the transformation chain on each panel below is the *same chain* you would write
against a live datasource. **No Prometheus or Loki is provisioned in this repo** — the
queries in every panel description and in the two query panels are reference copy, not
executed. Swap the datasource, paste the query, keep the transformations.

**Two queries in one panel** (edges + nodes, or two edge tiers) are separated with
`filter.byRefId` on each join. `refIdMatcher` is exact string equality, and the joined
output is stamped `refId: joinByField-A-A-…`, so a later `byRefId: "B"` cannot
re-capture it — both joins survive side by side.

panels.title: Service dependency map — graph
panels.description:
**Prometheus, two queries, two filtered joins.** Edges from the Tempo service-graph metrics; node colour from a per-service error ratio.

```promql
# A - edges\nsum by (client, server) (rate(traces_service_graph_request_total[$__rate_interval]))
```
```promql
# B - nodes: error ratio\n  sum by (server) (rate(traces_service_graph_request_failed_total[$__rate_interval]))
/ sum by (server) (rate(traces_service_graph_request_total[$__rate_interval]))
```
Each query joins under its own `filter.byRefId`, so refId A becomes the edges frame and refId B the nodes frame. Without the joins the panel would see one edge — `findEdgesFrame` reads only the first matching frame.

`payments-->gateway` closes a **cycle**. A graph draws it; the sankey panels alongside would have to hide such a link to stay acyclic, which is the whole reason to pick this variant for a dependency map.

Nodes are percentages against green/orange/red thresholds; one `byRegexp: /-->/` override flips every edge to req/s and back to a palette colour. That colour property is required, not cosmetic — an edge left on `thresholds` resolves a threshold colour instead of deferring to **Link color**. Pin the `gateway → catalogue` edge for its Explore link.

panels.title: Kubernetes CPU requests — sankey
panels.description:
**Prometheus, two edge queries, one unfiltered join.** Both refIds are edges and belong in the same frame, so there is nothing to keep apart.

```promql
# A - node -> namespace\nsum by (node, namespace) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="cpu"})
```
```promql
# B - namespace -> workload\nsum by (namespace, workload) (
  namespace_workload_pod:kube_pod_owner:relabel
    * on (namespace, pod) group_left()
      sum by (namespace, pod) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="cpu"})
)
```
Three tiers, conserved: 15 + 13 cores requested on the two nodes, 6 / 14 / 8 through the namespaces, the same out to the workloads. Because the flow balances, every ribbon width is directly comparable and no node shows a phantom surplus.

The fixture is a **DAG**, so no link is hidden to remove cycles and the panel shows no corner notice. Feed a sankey a cyclic topology and it will.

**A node's stat here is its degree, not its cores.** With only edge queries there is no nodes frame, so every node is *derived* from the endpoints and its value is its link count (`deriveNodesFromLinks`). A derived node has no field, so it formats with the panel **defaults** — which is why `cores` lives on an edges-only `byRegexp: /-->/` override instead: left on the defaults it would label `node-1` as `3.0 cores` when it requests 15. Canvas node values are off for the same reason. Add a third query (`sum by (node) (…)`) under its own `filter.byRefId` and the nodes become fields with real totals, the way the service map above colours its nodes.

panels.title: Cross-AZ request matrix — chord
panels.description:
**Prometheus, one query, one unfiltered join.** All nine ordered zone pairs from the Istio destination-side counter.

```promql
sum by (source_zone, destination_zone) (
  rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination"}[$__rate_interval])
)
```
Intra-AZ traffic dominates (the three self-loops); the cross-AZ ribbons in the 890–1450 band are the ones that carry a transfer charge. Chord takes **self-loops and cycles unchanged**, which is exactly why it fits a traffic matrix — a sankey would have to drop half of it.

Flavoured as an instant query: each series is a single flat value, so `mean` returns the fixture number exactly, the same as `lastNotNull` would.

`req/s` sits on an edges-only `byRegexp: /-->/` override, not on the defaults: with no nodes query every node is derived and its stat is its degree, which would otherwise read as a rate.

panels.title: The table route — graph, instant + label_join
panels.description:
**Prometheus, `Format: Table`, `Type: Instant`.** The other route: build the id in PromQL and pivot with core's **Rows to fields**.

```promql
label_join(
  sum by (client, server) (rate(traces_service_graph_request_total[$__range])),
  "id", ":", "client", "server"
)
```
`organize` runs filter → order → rename, so `indexByName`/`excludeByName` key on the **original** column names and `renameByName` runs last. `rowsToFields` then takes the first string column (`id`) as the field name, the first numeric one (`Value`) as its value, and drops everything else — `source`, `target` — into `field.labels`.

The ids deliberately join with `:` and contain **no** `-->`, so this panel proves the label carrier on its own: `endpointsOf` reads `field.labels` first and never reaches the name split. Same topology as the service map above, built a completely different way.

No `convertFieldType` step: `csv_content` already returns `Value` as a number, exactly as Prometheus does. Add one only when a column really does arrive as a string.

The `req/s` unit is attached by a `byRegexp: /:/` override — the same shape as the `/-->/` one on the service map, keyed to whatever this pivot happened to name the edges. Nodes are derived here, so their stat is a degree and is left unitless.

options.content:
LogQL metric queries return the **same** `timeseries-multi` shape as Prometheus, so the
first three panels reuse the recipe above unchanged — which is the point.

### 5 · Service call graph from structured logs — graph (panel below left)

```logql
sum by (service, upstream) (
  count_over_time({cluster="prod", namespace="ecommerce"} | logfmt | upstream != "" [$__auto])
)
```
`Legend: {{service}}-->{{upstream}}` · `Type: Range`

### 6 · Log volume by cluster → namespace → level — sankey (panel below right)

Two queries, one unfiltered join, both **instant**.

```logql
sum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({env="prod"} [$__range]))
```
`Legend: {{cluster}}-->{{namespace}}`

```logql
sum by (namespace, level) (count_over_time({env="prod"} | logfmt | level != "" [$__range]))
```
`Legend: {{namespace}}-->{{level}}`

### 7 · Page-transition matrix from ingress access logs — chord

```logql
sum by (referer_path, path) (
  count_over_time({job="ingress-nginx"} | logfmt | referer_path != "" | path != "" [$__range])
)
```
`Legend: {{referer_path}}-->{{path}}` · `Type: Instant`

### 8 · Parallel edges via `label_format` — graph

```logql
sum by (source, target, protocol) (
  count_over_time(
    {job="mesh/envoy"}
      | json
      | label_format source=`{{.source_workload}}`, target=`{{.destination_workload}}`
      | target != ""
    [$__range]
  )
)
```
`Legend: {{source}}->{{target}} ({{protocol}})` · `Type: Instant`

**`label_format` is doing the load-bearing work here.** It renames JSON fields into
real labels called `source` and `target`, which is what the contract reads endpoints
from. The legend deliberately uses `->`, *not* the `-->` separator, so the two
protocols over one pair stay **distinct field names** — two parallel edges — while both
still resolve to the same endpoints from their labels. A datasource that cannot emit
labels reaches the same place with an `extractFields` transformation.

panels.title: Service call graph from structured logs — graph
panels.description:
**Loki, range query, identical recipe to the Prometheus service map.** A LogQL metric query returns the same `timeseries-multi` shape, so the same single `joinByField` widens it — that equivalence is the point of this row.

```logql
sum by (service, upstream) (
  count_over_time({cluster="prod", namespace="ecommerce"} | logfmt | upstream != "" [$__auto])
)
```
An async order pipeline: `api → orders-worker → {inventory, billing}`, with `warehouse → orders-worker` closing a **retry loop**, plus the read path `api → search → catalogue-index`.

`sum` is the reducer, because a `count_over_time` series is a rate per bucket and the interesting number is the total over the window. Laid out `circular` — a second layout on the dashboard, and the one that makes the retry loop obvious.

panels.title: Log volume by cluster → namespace → level — sankey
panels.description:
**Loki, two instant queries, one unfiltered join.** Where the ingest bill goes.

```logql
# A - cluster -> namespace\nsum by (cluster, namespace) (count_over_time({env="prod"} [$__range]))
```
```logql
# B - namespace -> level\nsum by (namespace, level) (count_over_time({env="prod"} | logfmt | level != "" [$__range]))
```
Conserved across three tiers: each namespace's outflow to the levels sums to its inflow from the clusters (ecommerce 73 000, platform 18 000, observability 26 000), so the `info` ribbon width is honestly comparable with the `error` one. A **DAG** again, so nothing is hidden to remove cycles.

Instant-flavoured: single flat values, so `lastNotNull` returns the fixture number. Node values are off for the same reason as the CPU sankey — edges only, so a node's stat would be its degree rather than its log volume.

panels.title: Page-transition matrix from ingress access logs — chord
panels.description:
**Loki, one instant query.** Referer → path over the nginx ingress access log.

```logql
sum by (referer_path, path) (
  count_over_time({job="ingress-nginx"} | logfmt | referer_path != "" | path != "" [$__range])
)
```
Forward flow through `/home → /search → /product → /cart → /checkout`, two back-edges (`/product → /search`, `/cart → /product`), a loop close (`/checkout → /home`) and a **self-loop** on `/home` — a refresh. That reciprocal structure is what a chord exists for: every pair keeps both directions as separate ribbons.

Note the node ids are paths, and the edge id `/home-->/search` still splits correctly — but the endpoints come from `field.labels` anyway, which is the carrier that survives ids containing the separator.

panels.title: Parallel edges via label_format — graph
panels.description:
**Loki, one instant query, one join, no other transformation.** Two edges over the same node pair, separated only by a third label.

```logql
sum by (source, target, protocol) (
  count_over_time(
    {job="mesh/envoy"}
      | json
      | label_format source=`{{.source_workload}}`, target=`{{.destination_workload}}`
      | target != ""
    [$__range]
  )
)
```
`label_format` promotes the JSON fields to labels literally called `source` and `target` — the keys the contract reads endpoints from. The legend then uses `->`, which is **not** the separator (that is exactly `-->`), so `gateway->api (http)` and `gateway->api (grpc)` stay two distinct field names — two parallel edges — while both resolve to the same endpoints purely from their labels.

Each grpc edge carries `custom.lineType: dashed` and a curveness offset through an ordinary `byName` override, which is only addressable because an edge is a field. A datasource that cannot emit labels (Infinity, SQL returning `json`, quoted CSV) reaches the same place with an `extractFields` transformation in `json` format.
